Title: [LSJ] Optimal Seating Order - is it legal?

Messages.Author: Roger Carhult
Messages.Body:
At some tournaments the optimal seating order isn't used. The reason behind
this has been that it's said to be illegal according to the V:EKN rules
since seating of round 2 and 3 isn't random. Personally I don't agree with
this since the numbers are assigned randomly to begin with, so round 2 and 3
are random too. But I want to have it confirmed by LSJ that this is true. Is
optimal seating order

1) the most recommended seating method by WW and V:EKN,

2)just one among many methods

3) illegal in tournament play? (I'm sure this isn't the case but want it
explicitly clarified)

Roger

It is completely legal (and random), so long as the assigning of numbers to

LSJ made the optimal seating charts, you know. :-)

> 1) the most recommended seating method by WW and V:EKN,
>
> 2)just one among many methods
>
> 3) illegal in tournament play? (I'm sure this isn't the case but want it
> explicitly clarified)

2)

I personally recommend it for any 3-round (plus a final) V:TES tournament,
but it is not, AFAIK, the "official" recommendation. Any seating method
that is random and otherwise conforms to the V:EKN rules is sufficient. The
seating charts are just an aid, since making the seating designations
on-site can be difficult to do well.

Messages.Author: Gomi no Sensei
Messages.Body:
In article <a1vv9l$u0tap$1...@id-104455.news.dfncis.de>,
Roger Carhult <rogc...@student.luth.se> wrote:

>Ok it's late and I'm tired...obviously it must have been 9 people I never
>got to play. Since on round 1 I played 4 new people, round 2 I played 3 new
>people and round 3 I played another 3 new ones. That's 10 people + me so
>it's 20 - 11 = 9 people I never played. Why play 2 people twice when there's
>a whole nine I don't play at all? Obviously it's the same for all so it must
>be possible to make a seating order where you only play new people if you're
>as many as 20 players split on 4 tables.

Can't be done. Think of it this way: There are 4 tables, 1, 2, 3, 4.
Table 1 had 5 players: a, b, c, d, e, for round 1.

Round 2 comes along. You have 5 players and 4 tables. Try as you might, you
cannot avoid having one table with 2 people from Round 1 at it. Round 3
is just like round 2 -- there are 4 tables, and 5 people who played at table
1 in round 1, so there's no way not to have 2 people who played together
in round 1 at the same table in round 3.

Breaking it down:

You have a 3/4 chance of having an all-new table in Round 2, and a 3/4
chance again of an all-new table in round 3 = 9/16 chance of meeting
12 players throughout the tournament (meeting 4 new players at each of
3 tables).

You have a 6/16 ((3/4 * 1/4) + (1/4 * 3/4)) chance of meeting 11 new
players in the tournment (Round 1: meet 4 new players, Round 2 or 3:
meet 3 new players, Round 3 or 2: meet 4 new players).

You have a 1/16 (1/4 * 1/4) chance of meeting only 10 new players
(Round 1: meet 4 new, round 2: meet 3 new, round 3: meet 3 new).

So you were just unlucky =(.

Cheers,

gomi

I'm afraid that's as optimal as it gets, because for each round you're trying
to stuff 5 players into 4 tables so that people don't play each other more
than once. The leftover player has to wind up somewhere, so it's
unavoidable, unless your tournament has an attendance equal to a power of 5
(5, 25, or 125. How big do tournaments in France get? I don't think 125 yet).

The judge could always keep the seating order secret or something =) During
the tournaments I've played I've not experienced that people have looked
ahead and checked who they're going to meet in the next round until that
time has come. Even when I myself organized the Set's Call did I do that
even though I easily could. The thought didn't cross my mind and it felt
like it didn't matter anyway, I'd meet the people whether I liked it or not,
so knowing in advance wouldn't change anything. Perhaps people would be more
keen to figure out what decks other people are playing if they know who
they're going to meet, but it's not like they could ask friends who played
them to know anyway.

I don't have anything against randoming seating order each round, except
that you risk end up playing the same people (at different positions on the
table) in all three rounds. Something that happened in Gothenburg last time
too. We were only 10 people, and yet in three rounds I never played at the
same table as both Johan Hansson and Johan 'Bern' Carlsson (something I'm
glad of though since at least Hansson's deck seemed dangerous and I know
Bern's deck wasn't the best for my deck to meet either, but still it's not
fair for example Bern to have to face Hansson's deck three times when it won
all the three preliminary rounds). I think such a scenario is worse than
knowing who's gonna meet who the next round. Which could be solved in either
that the judge keeps the seating order secret or that it's published at
start to everybpdy has that info.

Roger C
